tips.title: Centre is double, semicircle is 90
tips.body: The angle at the **centre** is **twice** the angle at the circumference on the same arc. An angle in a **semicircle** is $90°$. Those two cover a large share of the questions.

tips.title: Look for the radius and the tangent
tips.body: A tangent meets a radius at $90°$. Two tangents from the same point are **equal**, which makes an isosceles triangle. Marking the right angles first often unlocks the rest of the diagram.

tips.title: Every step needs a named reason
tips.body: "Angles in the same segment are equal" earns the mark; "because it looks the same" does not. Write the theorem's name beside each step.

steps.title: The words, and the one fact underneath everything
steps.body:
Circle theorems are a set of facts about angles in circles, and the exam tests them in two ways: **calculate** an angle, and **give the reason** in the right words. The words matter, so start with the vocabulary.

- A **radius** joins the centre to the circle; a **diameter** goes right across through the centre.
- A **chord** joins two points on the circle without going through the centre.
- A **tangent** touches the circle at exactly one point.
- An **arc** is part of the circumference. An angle **subtended** by an arc has its vertex somewhere else and its arms ending on the arc's ends.
- A **segment** is the region cut off by a chord; a **sector** is the wedge between two radii.

And the fact underneath most proofs in this topic: **two radii make an isosceles triangle**. Whenever $O$ is joined to two points on the circle, the base angles are equal.

check.prompt: Which line joins two points on a circle without passing through the centre?
check.solution: A **chord**. A diameter is the special chord through the centre; a tangent touches the circle rather than crossing it.

steps.title: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
steps.body:
Take an arc $AB$. From the centre $O$, the arc makes angle $AOB$. From a point $C$ anywhere on the rest of the circle, it makes angle $ACB$. The theorem:

**The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, when both stand on the same arc.**

If angle $AOB = 130°$, angle $ACB = 65°$. Written as a reason: *angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference*.

The arc matters. Both angles must open onto the **same** arc. If $C$ moved onto the minor arc $AB$, its angle would stand on the major arc, and the centre angle to compare with would be the reflex one, $230°$, giving $115°$.

This teaching figure happens to be drawn to scale, so the $65°$ does look half the $130°$. Exam diagrams are **not** drawn accurately, so never measure one.

steps.title: The angle in a semicircle is 90°
steps.body:
A diameter splits the circle into two semicircles. Any point $C$ on the circle, joined to the two ends of the diameter, makes a **right angle**:

**The angle in a semicircle is $90°$.**

It is a special case of the last theorem. The diameter $AB$ is a straight line through $O$, so the angle at the centre is $180°$, and the angle at the circumference is half of that. Being able to say so is a proof, and it is on the specification.

In questions it usually appears as a hidden right angle: you are told $AB$ is a diameter and given one other angle in the triangle, and the third angle follows from $180°$.

steps.title: Angles in the same segment are equal
steps.body:
A chord $AB$ cuts the circle into two segments. Every angle drawn from the arc of one segment down to $A$ and $B$ is the same size:

**Angles in the same segment are equal.**

In the figure, angles $ACB$ and $ADB$ both stand on arc $AB$ from the same side, so they are equal. It follows from the centre theorem: both are half of the same angle at the centre.

The shape to look for is a **bow tie**: two chords crossing inside the circle. The angles at the two outer points that face the same arc are equal.

visuals.alt: Circle with chords AC, BC, AD and BD forming a bow tie; angles ACB and ADB both stand on arc AB and are equal, marked x

check.prompt: Angles $ACB$ and $ADB$ stand on the same arc $AB$. Angle $ACB = 58°$. What is angle $ADB$?
check.solution: Equal: $58°$, because angles in the same segment are equal.

steps.title: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°
steps.body:
A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on the circle.

**Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180°$.**

In $ABCD$, angle $A$ + angle $C = 180°$ and angle $B$ + angle $D = 180°$. Adjacent angles tell you nothing; it is the **opposite** pair every time.

Why: angle $A$ is half the arc $BCD$ and angle $C$ is half the arc $BAD$ (the centre theorem again), and those two arcs make up the whole circle, $360°$. Half of $360°$ is $180°$.

visuals.alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with angle BAD 100° and the opposite angle BCD 80°, adding to 180°

check.prompt: In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, angle $ADC = 95°$. What is angle $ABC$?
check.solution: $180 - 95 = 85°$: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180°$.

steps.title: Tangents: the right angle, and the equal pair
steps.body:
Two facts about tangents.

**A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at $90°$.** Whenever a question draws a tangent and joins the centre to the point of contact, there is a right angle, and it is nearly always the way in.

**Two tangents from the same external point are equal in length.** From $P$ outside the circle, the tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are the same length. With the two radii and the two right angles, $OAPB$ is a **kite**, and its four angles add to $360°$. That is how *find angle $AOB$* questions work: $360 - 90 - 90 - $ the angle at $P$.

Equal tangents also mean triangle $PAB$ is isosceles, which is often the second step.

In the figure the two points of contact are labelled $P_1$ and $P_2$; exam questions usually call them $A$ and $B$.

steps.title: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord
steps.body: **A line from the centre perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord in half.** It turns a chord question into **Pythagoras**: the radius is the hypotenuse, half the chord is one side, and the distance from the centre is the other.

Triangle $OMA$ is right-angled at $M$, with $OA = 10$ (radius)
$OM = 6$ cm

check.skill: perpendicular from the centre to a chord
check.solution: Half the chord is 12; radius $= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm.

steps.title: The alternate segment theorem
steps.body:
The last theorem is the one most people find hardest to *see*, so look at the figure before the words.

A tangent touches the circle at $A$. A chord $AB$ is drawn from the point of contact. The chord makes an angle with the tangent, and it also cuts the circle into two segments. The angle in the segment on the **other** side of the chord — the *alternate* segment — is equal to the angle between the tangent and the chord.

**The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.**

In the figure, the angle at $A$ between the tangent and chord $AB$, and the angle $ACB$ on the far side of the chord, are both $x$. To use it, find the chord that starts at the point of contact, and look across it.

visuals.alt: A tangent at A with chord AB; the angle between the tangent and the chord at A equals angle ACB in the alternate segment, both marked x

steps.title: Your turn: tangents and an isosceles triangle
steps.body: Tangents from $P$ touch the circle at $A$ and $B$, and angle $APB = 54°$. Find angle $OAB$. Do it on paper before revealing the lines; there are two routes, and both are worth knowing.

stages: Angle AOB = 360 − 90 − 90 − 54 = 126° (tangent and radius meet at 90°)
OA = OB, radii, so triangle OAB is isosceles
Or: PA = PB (equal tangents), so angle PAB = (180 − 54) ÷ 2 = 63°, and 90 − 63 = 27°

steps.title: Going deeper: proving a theorem, and the hidden isosceles
steps.body:
**Prove that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.** This is on the specification, and it is the model for every circle proof. Draw the diameter from $C$ through $O$. Triangles $OAC$ and $OBC$ are isosceles, because $OA = OB = OC$ are radii. Call their base angles $x$ and $y$. The **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, so angle $AOD = 2x$ and angle $BOD = 2y$. Then angle $AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x+y) = 2 \times$ angle $ACB$. Three facts do all the work: radii are equal, isosceles base angles are equal, exterior angle.

**The angle in a semicircle** is then a one-line corollary: the centre angle is $180°$, so the circumference angle is $90°$.

**Hidden isosceles triangles.** The hardest calculation questions rarely name a theorem you have not met; they hide two radii. Whenever you see $O$ joined to two points on the circle, write *isosceles, radii* before anything else.

**Algebra inside a theorem.** *Angle $BAC = 2x$, angle $ABC = 3x$, $AB$ a diameter*: the theorem gives the $90°$, the angle sum gives $5x + 90 = 180$.

visuals.alt: The proof figure: C on the circumference with the diameter CD drawn through the centre O, radii to A and B, so that triangles OAC and OBC are isosceles with base angles x and y

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Angle at the centre** is twice the angle at the circumference, on the same arc.
- **Angle in a semicircle** is $90°$.
- **Angles in the same segment** are equal (the bow tie).
- **Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral** add to $180°$.
- **Tangent and radius** meet at $90°$; **two tangents** from a point are equal, making a kite with the radii.
- **Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord**: then Pythagoras.
- **Alternate segment**: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
- **Two radii make an isosceles triangle**: the hidden step in most hard questions.
- **Reasons** are marks: name the theorem in its standard words, every step.

questions.prompt: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. Angle $AOB = 100°$. Find angle $ACB$, where $C$ is on the major arc.
questions.solution: The angle at the centre is **twice** the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so angle $ACB = 100 \div 2 = 50°$.

questions.prompt: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is a point on the circumference. Angle $CAB = 32°$. Find angle $ABC$.
questions.solution: The angle in a semicircle is $90°$, so angle $ACB = 90°$. Angles in a triangle: $180 - 90 - 32 = 58°$.

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle $ABC = 112°$. Find angle $ADC$.
questions.solution: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180°$: $180 - 112 = 68°$.

questions.prompt: A tangent touches a circle at $T$, and $O$ is the centre. What is the angle between the tangent and the radius $OT$?
questions.solution: A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at **right angles**, always.

questions.prompt: Two tangents from a point $P$ touch a circle with centre $O$ at $A$ and $B$. Angle $APB = 48°$. Find angle $AOB$.
questions.solution: The tangent meets each radius at $90°$, so $OAPB$ is a quadrilateral with two right angles. Its angles add to $360°$: $360 - 90 - 90 - 48 = 132°$.

questions.prompt: A chord of length 16 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 10 cm. Find the distance from the centre to the chord.
questions.skill: perpendicular from the centre to a chord
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the centre **bisects** the chord, so it meets the chord 8 cm from each end. That makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 (the radius) and one side 8: the distance is $\sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm.

questions.prompt: $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on a circle. Chords $AC$ and $BD$ cross. Angle $CAD = 41°$. Find angle $CBD$.
questions.solution: Angles $CAD$ and $CBD$ both stand on the arc $CD$, so they are in the **same segment** and equal: $41°$.

questions.prompt: A tangent touches a circle at $A$. $B$ and $C$ are points on the circle, and the angle between the tangent and the chord $AB$ is $57°$. Find angle $ACB$, where $C$ is in the alternate segment.
questions.solution: The **alternate segment theorem**: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. So angle $ACB = 57°$.

questions.prompt: $O$ is the centre of a circle and $A$ and $B$ are on the circumference. Angle $OAB = 28°$. Find angle $AOB$.
questions.solution: $OA$ and $OB$ are both radii, so triangle $OAB$ is **isosceles** and angle $OBA = 28°$ too. Then angle $AOB = 180 - 28 - 28 = 124°$. Two radii always make an isosceles triangle: it is the most used fact in the topic that is not officially a theorem.

questions.prompt: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. Angle $ABC = 64°$. Work out angle $AOC$ (the angle at the centre standing on the arc $AC$ that does not contain $B$). Give a reason for each step.
questions.skill: angle at the centre with reasons
questions.solution: One theorem, one reason: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so angle $AOC = 2 \times 64 = 128°$. The reason has to be written in words the examiner recognises.

questions.prompt: Prove that the angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
questions.solution: Draw the diameter from the circumference point $C$ through $O$ to $D$. Triangles $OAC$ and $OBC$ are isosceles (radii). In triangle $OAC$, angles $OAC = OCA = x$, so the exterior angle $AOD = 2x$. Likewise $BOD = 2y$. So angle $AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x+y) = 2 \times$ angle $ACB$. The proof lives on two facts: radii make isosceles triangles, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles.

questions.modelAnswer: Draw the line from $C$ through $O$ to the point $D$ on the circle. $OA = OC$ (radii), so triangle $OAC$ is isosceles and angle $OAC =$ angle $OCA = x$. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, so angle $AOD = 2x$. In the same way $OB = OC$, angle $OBC =$ angle $OCB = y$, and angle $BOD = 2y$. So angle $AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y)$, and angle $ACB = x + y$. Therefore the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.

questions.prompt: Two tangents from $P$ touch a circle with centre $O$ at $A$ and $B$. Angle $APB = 54°$. Find angle $OAB$.
questions.solution: Angle $AOB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 54 = 126°$ (two right angles between tangent and radius). Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles (radii), so angle $OAB = (180 - 126) \div 2 = 27°$. Alternatively: $PA = PB$ (equal tangents), so angle $PAB = 63°$, and $OAB = 90 - 63 = 27°$.

questions.prompt: A tangent touches a circle with centre $O$ at $A$. $B$ is on the circle and angle $OAB = 34°$. Find the angle between the tangent and the chord $AB$.
questions.solution: The tangent and the radius $OA$ meet at $90°$, and the chord sits inside that right angle: $90 - 34 = 56°$.

questions.prompt: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is a point on the circumference. Prove that angle $ACB = 90°$.
questions.skill: proof of the angle in a semicircle
questions.solution: Either use the angle at the centre theorem: angle $AOB = 180°$ (a straight line), so the angle at the circumference is half of it, $90°$. Or from scratch: $OA = OB = OC$ (radii), so triangles $OAC$ and $OBC$ are isosceles with base angles $x$ and $y$; the angles of triangle $ABC$ give $2x + 2y = 180°$, so $x + y = 90°$, which is angle $ACB$.

questions.modelAnswer: $AB$ is a diameter, so $AOB$ is a straight line and angle $AOB = 180°$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so angle $ACB = 180 \div 2 = 90°$.

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral and $O$ is the centre. Angle $BOD = 140°$ (the angle on the arc containing $C$). Which is angle $BAD$?
questions.skill: centre theorem inside a cyclic quadrilateral
questions.solution: Angle $BAD$ is at the circumference on the same arc $BCD$ as the centre angle of $140°$, so it is $70°$. (Angle $BCD$, on the other side, is then $110°$: opposite angles add to $180°$.)

questions.prompt: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are on a circle with centre $O$. $AB$ is a diameter, and angle $BAC = 2x$ and angle $ABC = 3x$. Work out $x$, giving reasons.
questions.skill: forming an equation from a theorem
questions.solution: Angle $ACB = 90°$ (angle in a semicircle). The angles in the triangle add to $180°$: $2x + 3x + 90 = 180$, so $5x = 90$ and $x = 18$.

criteria.text: Angle ACB = 90°, with the reason: angle in a semicircle
Equation 5x + 90 = 180 from the angle sum of a triangle

questions.modelAnswer: The angle in a semicircle is $90°$, so angle $ACB = 90°$. The angles in a triangle add to $180°$, so $2x + 3x + 90 = 180$, giving $5x = 90$ and $x = 18$.

questions.prompt: A circle has radius 13 cm. A chord is 5 cm from the centre. Find the length of the chord.
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord and makes a right-angled triangle with the radius as hypotenuse: half the chord is $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm, so the chord is $24$ cm. Forgetting to double is the usual slip.

examTechnique.body:
Circle theorem questions carry two kinds of mark: the angle, and the reason. The reason must name the theorem in recognisable words, so learn the eight phrases in the summary as sentences and write one after every angle you find. A correct angle with no reason usually scores half.

The diagrams are not drawn accurately, so measuring is useless; the theorems do the work. Look first for a diameter (a hidden right angle), then for two radii (a hidden isosceles triangle), then for a tangent (a right angle with the radius). Multi-step questions chain two or three of these, and the proof of the centre theorem is on the specification, so be able to write it from memory.
examinerErrors: Giving the angle without the reason, or a vague reason such as *because of the circle theorem*.
Halving the wrong angle: the centre and circumference angles must stand on the same arc.
Using adjacent angles of a cyclic quadrilateral instead of opposite ones.
Missing the isosceles triangle made by two radii.
Forgetting to halve the chord before using Pythagoras, or forgetting to double afterwards.
In the alternate segment theorem, matching the tangent-chord angle to the angle on the same side of the chord instead of the far side.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states every angle with its theorem in standard words, spots the hidden right angle from a diameter or tangent and the hidden isosceles triangle from two radii, and chains theorems through a multi-step problem without losing the thread. It can prove the angle at the centre theorem from isosceles triangles and the exterior angle, derive the semicircle result from it, and set up and solve an equation when the angles are given in terms of x.
